I am a 28 year old female diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder with severe dissociative symptoms. Despite being high-functioning, I have been hospitalized three times in locked psychiatric units. In addition to other applicable diagnoses, I have been misdiagnosed with Schizophrenia and subsequently spent months as a living zombie due to incorrect medication.

I wanted to do this AMA in hopes that I can shed a little bit of light on the stigma associated with Borderline and how real life with the disorder differs from the sensationalized depictions described online or in media. It is so upsetting to see that online advice for someone concerned about dating someone with Borderline is simply: RUN. RUN AS FAST AS YOU CAN. Society's caricature of the disorder make it easy to feel ashamed and isolate yourself.

I'm happy to answer any question at all. Thanks!
I have Borderline Personality Disorder. AMA!
What has been the one thing, or main things, that you feel like has been your anchor or carried you through all the hard times?

That's a real great question. With Borderline, you can get rapid fluctuations of extreme emotions that sometimes leave you feeling so, so down. I've found that keeping a notebook to just write things, anything, down has been something I've done consistently through the roughest of times. Sometimes I'm scrawling suicide notes, or drawing what looks like very intricate doodles that, at the time, was the only way I could release how I was feeling. But the most helpful thing I found was looking up Buddhist quotes that related to however I was feeling and writing them in my notebook. I was raised Catholic and am non-practicing, but for some reason Buddhist quotes have always given me comfort.
That's really cool. Just out of curiosity, not as a suggestion, have you thought of or tried a video journal?

You know, I've never actually thought about that... but it's a really interesting idea!! I am a bit camera shy, even if it would just be for me, but I think that could be incredibly insightful. I did my undergrad in psychology, it could be like doing a case study on myself! May I ask what made you think of that?

I try to regularly keep a video journal, and I mostly speak as if my kids, 30 years from now, are all sitting around me and I'm recounting an old story.

I feel like so much can be lost, by me, in writing because I don't always know how to succinctly put what I'm thinking and body language is so very insightful.

Thats amazing! I would really like to try it out. My psychiatrist specializes in Transfocused Psychotherapy and he will often point out my body language and other non-verbal clues. Sometimes what my body is saying completely contradicts what is coming out of my mouth. It can be such mindfuck lol but I think it has been invaluable

I hope it is useful to you, the hardest part for me is the days that I really don't feel like recording myself. Those are usually the most telling sessions when it comes to seeing who I am.

Sometimes I watch old videos of myself and remember that I had a particularly good or bad day the day I recorded myself and subtle or not so subtle body language will indicate it.

Wow, that is so fascinating. I guess I would actually be able to see what my doctor sees in our sessions. Like you said, usually the most intense sessions are those that I don't think I have anything to talk about. Do you do the video journals for another reason other than to document your life?

One other reason is, well, therapeutic. I've found that it can help me work out what the root cause of problems I've having with my mood.

As an example, a few months ago I had a two week period where I really was just having a hard time with everything, I felt completely out of sync with my life. I normally could just jump out of bed at 6:00 am and crank out code for six hours (I work from home) without any issue. For that two weeks I felt like I just couldn't do it, and every day it was a pain to wake up and start working. Talking about my problems on a video gave me time to really focus on my situation, and it turns out that most of my side projects had been going stale for a few months because I never had or made time to work on them. I hadn't made any progress on things I wanted to work on outside of my day job, and it was getting to me more than I thought. So I spent an evening just doing what I wanted to, and I didn't stress over how perfect the code was. I focused on getting something working that could make me feel accomplished. The very next day I snapped out of it.

That's really amazing. I'm so happy that it works for you. It's also really great that you are able to self-analyze so positively. I think a lot of people have difficulty recognizing areas where fault may lay with them and would rather blame it on something external. You could be a great therapist if you ever want to change careers! I bet you are a great listener and motivator to loved ones :)

When you look back, what are the best things friends and family have done to support you? And what are the least helpful things? I'm close to someone with BPD and want to know how I can be a better friend.

It's tough because she looks to me for approval a lot. On the one hand I want to be as accepting as possible, because she carries a lot of guilt and embarrassment about her mental issues and struggles to feel good about herself. But on the other hand, she makes a lot of poor decisions and I don't want to condone her just letting her untreated illness hang out. I've been somewhat successful in setting boundaries without losing her, and want to keep up this track record!

Thanks for doing this AMA.

You're a great friend. It must be difficult to find a middle ground, but its important to set boundaries.

I think that the best thing that anyone has done for me has also been the hardest for me. My boyfriend is very understanding but will also hold me accountable for my actions. Instead of just letting me wiggle my way out of it, he helps me realize that I was being irrational or I overreacted. We've learned through trial and error that it is most helpful after I've calmed down a bit. It is hard but I want to get everything under control so I am willing to look my faults in the eye and make changes.

Even though my parents mean well, they completely baby me and feed into the perception I have of myself as helpless and fragile which is my comfort zone. Although it definitely feels good, I think their lack of boundaries has made it difficult to change at times. I've gotten away with so much and them not stepping and saying that its not ok allows me to rationalize my slip ups.

Approval seeking is definitely a thing I struggle with as well. Very often I take any action or make any decisions because I feel that I can't until someone says that its right or that they agree. Try to find some way to empower her and remind her that she is a solid, capable person that can be decisive and effective. I have a lot of guilt and embarrassment too and haven't really told anyone, which is why I wanted to do this AMA so I could get feel more comfortable with it. Like I said before, being held accountable for my actions has really helped me but she has to be willing to see that maybe she was wrong in a certain situation or could have handled something better. Is she in therapy? DBT is a great place to start. I think you should also make your boundaries very clear to her and don't flip flop on them. If she crosses a boundary, remind her of it and show her how she's crossed it that situation.

I'm here anytime if you want to PM me just to talk and get the other side of things :)
Have you ever cheated on your SO because of ups and downs of bpd?

No, never. This is one thing that makes me especially upset. Being unfaithful or sexually promiscuous is included in almost every description of BPD. I find it very unfair that I have to reassure my boyfriend that I have been nothing but loyal, not because my actions have created doubt but because it is included in the vast majority of depictions. I'm not sure if I'm an anomaly, but I have always been a serial monogamist.
What is the best therapy tools that you have learned to help yourself?

DBT has been really helpful, especially the emotion regulation, distress tolerance and mindfulness modules. The practice of distraction taught in distress tolerance has been something I've found myself utilizing often. With BPD, a lot of very strong emotions can come up and instead of discharging them into unhealthy channels, distracting myself with maybe a long hot shower, watching cute cat videos or a funny movie, have helped me ride the waves until those overwhelming feelings have passed.
What does it feel like on a "low?" do you realize it is a low?

A low for me feels as though I am the worst, most terrible person on the face of the planet and not one single person cares about me. I get this overwhelming feeling of self hatred and a deep loneliness that I can feel down to the bone. I feel that everything is utterly hopeless and that I am doomed to suffer a painless pain forever. It has taken me a lot of work to be able to recognize that the feeling is temporary and that a lot of the thoughts/feeling I have about myself or others is mostly not based in fact. I still struggle with being able to identify the situations as they happen. My psychiatrist says that when I experience a strong emotion like a low or anger, that feeling becomes all consuming and I'm unable to process any other data from the situation. I can only focus on that emotion and my mind runs away with it.
